Distinct functional responses of producers and consumers to climate generate functional trophic assymmetry

Analysis considering GEB reviewer concerns

This notebook summarizes analytical choices and sensitivity analysis to review previous to update the manuscript text.

1 Original patterns

1.1 Geographic patterns in Functional Diversity and FTA

We calculated functional richness (FRic) and functional dispersion (FDis) separately for palms and mammals in each province. Each value was standardized against richness-preserving random assemblages to obtain SES.

FTA was defined as mammal SES minus palm SES.

Positive FTA indicates that mammals are relatively more functionally diverse than palms, given each group’s species richness and regional species pool. Negative FTA indicates the opposite.

1.2 Original FTA ~ climate relationships

The original climate models related present-day functional diversity and FTA to current climate and historical anomalies. The original models included current climate and both historical anomalies as predictors.

2 Reviewer concenrs

2.1 Climate-model choices and diagnostics

Historical climate anomalies are calculated by subtracting current climate from past climate. Reviewers noted that including both current climate and these anomalies in the same model may therefore make their associations with FTA difficult to separate.

The figures below show the correlations among predictors and how BIOCLIM variables are represented in each of the PCA axis. Note we fitted separate PCAs to each predictor.

  • Correlations
  • Climate PCA loadings

2.1.1 Model concurvity

Reviewers suggested to check model concurvity (i.e. How much one model term can be explained by the other terms).

The reviewer was right in their concern of how confidently we can attribute the fitted patterns to individual predictors. The table below shows that concurvity was indeed high (>0.7) and highest when geography was included. This indicated that some climate and spatial effects were difficult to separate.

Table 1. Diagnostics for the original three-period climate models. Concurvity near one indicates that a fitted term overlaps strongly with other terms.

2.2 Selecting candidate models to address concurvity issues

To address the reviewers concerns, I fitted additional model candidates to test them for concurvity: current climate, each anomaly separately, and current climate with each anomaly. Each was fitted with and without geography using the same provinces and original FTA.

Evaluating model candidates
  • Model specification: Whether geography is included alongside climate.
  • Provinces: Number of provinces used to fit the model.
  • Effective df: Model complexity; higher values indicate more flexible relationships.
  • Adjusted R²: How much variation in FTA the model explains, accounting for complexity.
  • Deviance explained: The proportion of variation in FTA explained by the model.
  • AIC: A balance between fit and complexity; lower values indicate a better-supported model among those compared.
  • Max. concurvity: The greatest overlap between a model term and the other predictors; values near 1 indicate strong overlap.
  • Residual Moran I: How strongly unexplained values are spatially clustered.
  • Moran p: Whether that spatial clustering is greater than expected by chance.

Table 2. Candidate climate models fitted to original FTA.

For additional spatial validation, I also divided the provinces into geographic groups based on proximity (4 groups) and tested how well the model predicted each group using a model fit on the remaining ones (i.e. spatial-block predictions)

Table 3. Spatial-block prediction errors. Lower RMSE means better prediction

2.2.1 Choosing a model to carry forward for further sensitivity tests

In the following figure you can use selectors to check each candidate models. Select a model and FTA measure.

Fitted climate terms for the selected candidate model. Lines show centered effects with and without geography; bands are approximate 95% pointwise intervals.

While our climate-FTA patterns seem relatively robust to model selection, the following sensitivity analysies will use current climate + LGM anomaly without geography. It was selected because it predicted the held-out blocks better than current + Late Holocene, although neither clearly improved FRic prediction over the baseline.

All models with geography had high concurvity, therefore were not considered in the following steps.

3 Sensitivity analyses

3.1 To palm PCoA dimensionality and species pool choices

Following JP’s suggestion, we compare the original separate species pools with a shared geographic pool, using the same source provinces to draw palms and mammals. In addition, as the reviewer point out, we test for palm-trait space dimensionality (adding axis to the first palm PCoA to compute FD)

Therefore, this test compare original FTA with three alternatives:

  • a geographic species pool,

  • two palm axes,

  • both changes together.

The pool includes the focal province and eight nearby sources selected using a 500 km distance-decay scale. Two palm axes allow FD to describe an area instead of a range.

The selected current + LGM model was fitted to each FTA version using the same provinces within each measure.

  • FRic — PC1
  • FRic — PC2
  • FDis — PC1
  • FDis — PC2

3.2 To province-assigment sensitivity

The reviewers also express concern on the model sensitivity to the species biogeographic province assigment rules. The original rule assigned species to a province when at least 5% of their range cells fell there, excluding layers with fewer than ten occupied cells.

To address the reviewers’ concerns, I varied the minimum range overlap from 5% to 1% and 10%, and the minimum number of occupied cells from 10 to 5 and 20, then recalculated FTA. The trait spaces and null pools remained fixed. Then, I re-fitted the selected current + LGM model to each membership rule.

Table 4. FTA under alternative rules compared with the reconstructed original rule.

  • FDis — PC1
  • FDis — PC2
  • FRic — PC1
  • FRic — PC2

Generally, FTA-FDis was relatively stable across the tested province-membership rules, whereas FTA-FRic was more sensitive to the range-overlap threshold.

4 Evaluating the links between FTA and interaction network assembly

Reviewers also express concern whether and how FTA is linked to interaction traits and network structure.

Realistically, though, data local interaction networks are not available. Therefore, I could not directly test whether FTA predicts network assembly (whithout relying on the complex inputation methods). However, I think we can address the reviewer concerns using only those available metaweb interactions from the species subsets of each of the biogeographic provinces, both for palms and mammals separately. In other words, we can ‘estimate’ biogeographic province interaction niches by measuring the trait space that provincial palm/mammal assemblages occupy in the continental metaweb.

4.1 Does the metaweb represent biogeographic province trait diversity?

I assessed whether how well partner traits in the metaweb are represented in each province, by:

  1. Collecting the metaweb partners of the province’s palms and mammals, counting each partner species once.

  2. Calculating the fraction of those partners that occur in the province.

  3. For each absent partner, finding the province species with the most similar measured traits.

  4. Averaging those trait distances. Lower distances indicate that similar partner traits are present in the province.

  • FRic
  • FDis

Table 6. Exploratory associations between FTA and partner representation, adjusted for richness, coverage and geography. Adjusted p-values account for eight comparisons.

4.2 Does FTA relate to the observed diversity of interaction partners across trophic levels?

To answer this question, I assessed how regional FTA relates to metaweb functional diversity, by:

  1. Identifying the palms and mammals occurring in each province.

  2. Collecting the set of documented partners from the continental metaweb, regardless if those partners occur or not in the focal province.

  3. Measuring the functional diversity of the assemblage of interaction partners in the metaweb (a.k.a. potential functional interaction niche)

  4. Comparing the estimated provincial interaction niche with FTA across provinces.

FTA adjustment

To account for differences among provinces, I used regression to remove the variation in FTA and partner diversity associated with palm and mammal richness, metaweb coverage and location. A positive adjusted FTA means the province is more mammal-biased than expected given these factors; a negative value means it is more palm-biased than expected.

Table 5. Associations between FTA and documented regional partner diversity using two palm axes. Null p-values compare the observed relationship with degree-preserving rearrangements of the continental metaweb.

The clearest trend is that provinces with more functionally clustered mammal partners of palms (a.k.a. functional interaction niches) tend to have more mammal-biased FTA-FDis. Provinces with more dispersed mammal partners tend to have more palm-biased FTA-FDis. However, this trend was not clearly different from the network-randomization baseline (null p = 0.27; adjusted p = 0.69). We could increase the sampling draws for the null model for publication, but I do not expect the significance to vary.

4.3 Does FTA relate to guild connectivity?

To asses whether FTA produces more connected networks, I averaged the expected connectivity across the guilds represented in each province by:

  1. Calculating the fraction of its metaweb-represented palms and mammals belonging to each guild.

  2. Taking the regional SBM connection probability for every palm–mammal guild combination.

  3. Averaging those probabilities, weighted by the proportion of represented species in that guild.

Note

As a reminder, a SBM groups species into guilds according to their recorded interaction patterns. It then estimates how likely each palm guild is to interact with each mammal guild.

For each province, expected connectivity is the average of those regional interaction probabilities, weighted by how common each guild is among the province’s metaweb-represented species. A higher value means the province contains more palms and mammals belonging to species groups that frequently interact across the metaweb.
